A subordinate is a person who is below someone else in rank or authority within a structured system — like a company, the military, a government, or any organization with a clear hierarchy.

If you are someone's subordinate, it means that person has authority over you. You work under them, take direction from them, and are answerable to them.

The word "subordinate" always implies a two-sided relationship:

  • One person has more authority → they are called the superior
  • The other person has less authority → they are called the subordinate

A subordinate follows the instructions, orders, or guidance of their superior. The superior has the power to assign tasks, evaluate performance, give promotions, or even let the subordinate go.

Think of it this way: if someone tells you what to do at work and you're expected to listen to them, you are their subordinate.
A simple example to make it click

Imagine a company:

CEO → Department Head → Manager → Team Member

In this chain:

  • The Team Member is a subordinate of the Manager.
  • The Manager is a subordinate of the Department Head.
  • The Department Head is a subordinate of the CEO.

Notice something important here: the same person can be both a superior and a subordinate at the same time, depending on who you're comparing them to. The Manager is a subordinate to the Department Head, but a superior to the Team Member.
How it's used in a sentence

• "The general gave orders to his subordinates."
    → The general is in command; the people below him in military rank must follow his orders.
  • "She was a kind leader who always listened to her subordinates."
    → "Her subordinates" = the people who work under her in the company.
  • "As a new employee, he was a subordinate with very little decision-making power."
    → He was low in the hierarchy and had to follow others' decisions.
  • "The manager delegated the project to her subordinates."
    → She passed the work down to the people below her.
Where you'll commonly encounter this word

1. The workplace — This is where you'll see it most often. Employees are subordinates to their managers. Junior staff are subordinates to senior staff.

2. The military — Soldiers are subordinates to officers. Lower-ranking officers are subordinates to higher-ranking ones. In the military, being a subordinate is very formal — you must follow commands without question.

3. Government and bureaucracy — Junior officials are subordinates to senior officials. A deputy minister, for example, is a subordinate to the minister.

4. Any organization with ranks — Schools, hospitals, religious institutions, sports teams with coaching staff — anywhere there's a structured hierarchy, the word can apply.
What the word does NOT mean

It does not mean the person is less intelligent, less capable, or less important as a human being. It is a purely structural term — it only describes where someone sits in a chain of authority. A highly skilled expert can be someone's subordinate simply because of the organizational chart, not because of their talent or knowledge.

Also, being a subordinate does not mean you have no power at all. Within their own area of work, subordinates often make many decisions independently. The word only tells you that someone above them holds ultimate authority.
A subtle but important point: "direct subordinate"

You may sometimes hear the phrase "direct subordinate". This refers to someone who reports immediately to a person — with no one in between.

For example, if a CEO has three vice presidents reporting directly to her, those three are her direct subordinates. All the thousands of employees below them in the company are also technically her subordinates, but not direct ones — there are layers of management in between.

"Subordinate" is a formal, professional word. In casual everyday speech, people tend to use simpler alternatives like:

  • "My team"
  • "The people who work under me"
  • "My juniors"
  • "My reports" (short for "direct reports," common in corporate settings)

But in formal writing, official documents, management literature, military communications, or any discussion of organizational structure, "subordinate" is the precise and preferred term.

A subordinate is a person who ranks below another in a hierarchy and is under that person's authority — required to follow their direction, answer to them, and carry out their assignments within the structure of an organization.
